Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base

Wenqing Wang    Joonghyuk Shin Affiliation: Seoul National University    Jonathan Tremblay    Chan Hee Song    Yun Fu Affiliation: Northeastern University Affiliation: NVIDIA
Abstract

Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ∼95%{\sim}95\% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model’s own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces Δ\Delta-drift from +11.3+11.3 to +1.65+1.65 without real video and to −0.16\mathbf{-0.16} with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57+3.57 with over 𝟏𝟓𝟎×\mathbf{150\times} less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

1 Introduction

Video diffusion models (Wan Team, 2025; Polyak et al., 2024) generate high-quality clips, making them promising for live content creation, simulation, and interactive world modeling. However, most use bidirectional attention (Yin et al., 2025) and jointly denoise a clip whose length is fixed before generation begins. Playback therefore cannot begin until the clip has been generated. This inherently limits their applicability to real-time streaming and long-horizon video generation.

Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models address some of these limitations by generating frames in chunks, with each chunk conditioned on those generated before it (Chen et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Sand.ai, 2025; Skywork AI, 2025). This allows rollouts of flexible length and lets playback begin before generation is complete. However, models trained to continue from clean context must condition on their own imperfect outputs at inference. Errors are therefore fed back into subsequent chunks and accumulate over time, often causing the video to drift toward oversaturated, textureless frames within seconds (drift; Fig. 1, top). This train–inference mismatch, known as exposure bias (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Po et al., 2025), remains a central challenge for AR video generation.

Existing drift-reduction methods fall into three categories. Base retraining incorporates the model’s own rollouts into training (Huang et al., 2025; Po et al., 2025), which is effective but expensive: the strongest published result uses 136136K clips and 16×16{\times}H100 GPUs (Po et al., 2025). Training-free methods keep the weights fixed and modify inference by noising the context (Chen et al., 2024; Skywork AI, 2025), guiding generation against a cleaner history (Song et al., 2025), correcting the sampling trajectory (Xiang et al., 2026), or managing the cache (Meng et al., 2026). These methods either treat drift as uniform noise or re-anchor generation to a prediction that multi-step models do not produce, and none that we evaluate reduces drift at 50 s (§5). Frozen-base correctors learn lightweight corrections, but existing methods target sampling noise (Yu et al., 2025) or cache-approximation error (Peng et al., 2025), rather than error induced by generated history. Thus, deployed checkpoints still lack an efficient learned correction that directly targets exposure-bias drift.

In this paper, we introduce Clean Forcing, an efficient drift-reduction method for frozen AR video diffusion models. We first characterize history-induced drift by holding a noisy state ztz_{t} fixed and comparing the model’s denoising velocities under drifted and clean histories. This counterfactual isolates the error induced by the generated history, and our analysis shows that ∼95%{\sim}95\% of the resulting velocity gap is consistent across noise seeds, indicating that drift is largely systematic and learnable. Based on this insight, we train a rank-16 LoRA corrector rϕr_{\phi} (5.95.9M parameters, 0.4%0.4\% of the base) to predict this velocity gap while keeping the base model frozen. To expose the corrector to states induced by its own predictions, we introduce a closed-loop stage that regenerates training pairs with the corrector active (Ross et al., 2011) and penalizes the downstream drift caused by each committed prediction. The base model’s own single-shot generations serve as clean references, so training requires no real videos. On a lightly adapted causal Wan2.1-1.3B (Wan Team, 2025), Clean Forcing reduces Δ\Delta-drift from +11.3+11.3 to −0.16-0.16 over 50 s on 128 MovieGen prompts (Polyak et al., 2024). Without real videos, it achieves +1.65+1.65, outperforming the best published result of +3.57+3.57 (Po et al., 2025) while using over 150×150\times less data. The corrector trains in one GPU-day and merges into the base model without adding inference overhead.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify that the velocity error induced by a drifted history is largely systematic across noise seeds, which makes the drift correction learnable.

  • •

    We introduce Clean Forcing, a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector trained on a frozen base model to match clean-history predictions at the same noisy state. Training combines a closed-loop stage for DAgger aggregation and drift contraction with a self-teaching procedure that requires no real videos.

  • •

    Clean Forcing eliminates measurable drift using far less data than base retraining and adds no inference overhead. Among the compared methods, it achieves the lowest drift and highest aesthetic score, while ranking second in subject and background consistency, imaging quality, and MUSIQ. It also transfers to an independent base, scales to a 10×10\times larger base, and reduces drift in two other AR world models.

2 Related Work

Video Generation. Early video generation used GANs (Vondrick et al., 2016; Tulyakov et al., 2018) or autoregressed over discrete visual tokens (Yan et al., 2021). GANs offered fast sampling but were difficult to train, while token-based models faced growing generation costs as video sequences lengthened. Diffusion models (Ho et al., 2022b; Blattmann et al., 2023) improved training stability and visual quality, enabling large-scale systems such as (Brooks et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2024; Wan Team, 2025; Polyak et al., 2024). Most of these models jointly denoise a predetermined clip with bidirectional spatiotemporal attention (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Ho et al., 2022a; Bar-Tal et al., 2024). Joint denoising promotes temporal coherence, but requires a fixed clip length and delays playback until the full clip is generated, limiting real-time streaming and long-horizon generation.

Autoregressive Video Diffusion. AR diffusion generates video in chunks, enabling streaming and flexible-length rollouts. However, training on clean histories but conditioning on imperfect outputs at inference creates exposure bias, causing errors to compound into drift. To address this mismatch, Diffusion Forcing trains on frames with different noise levels (Chen et al., 2024), a formulation that DFoT extends to transformers with guidance over the generated history (Song et al., 2025). Self Forcing takes a different route by training on the model’s rollouts (Huang et al., 2025). For interactive generation, CausVid distills a bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal student (Yin et al., 2025), an approach further developed by Causal Forcing (Zhu et al., 2026). MAGI-1 adds noise to clean context during training to reduce exposure bias (Sand.ai, 2025), while SkyReels-V2 uses Diffusion Forcing and noised, overlapping context to improve long-video consistency (Skywork AI, 2025). These methods mitigate error accumulation without isolating the prediction error caused by the generated history. In contrast, Clean Forcing uses the frozen model’s own generations to learn the velocity gap between clean and drifted histories at the same noisy state, reducing drift while preserving streaming, flexible-length rollouts, and inference speed.

Mitigating Exposure Bias. In imitation learning, errors caused by visiting self-generated states are addressed by collecting training examples from the learner’s own rollouts (Ross et al., 2011). Video generation methods take a similar approach by retraining the base on its outputs, using distributional targets (Huang et al., 2025), reversed rollouts (Po et al., 2025), and large-scale rollout training (Liu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025). This improves long-horizon stability, but requires a full model update and 10410^{4}–105+10^{5}{+} clips. Concurrent work post-trains few-step generators on matched-state targets from real videos (Liu et al., 2026). Training-free methods instead noise the context (Chen et al., 2024; Skywork AI, 2025), guide generation with a cleaner history (Song et al., 2025), adjust the sampling path or activations (Xiang et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2026), or manage the cache (Meng et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2025). They require no training, but do not reliably reduce drift (§5). Frozen-base correctors offer a lightweight alternative, but AutoRefiner targets sampling noise (Yu et al., 2025), while ERTACache addresses the separate problem of cache-approximation error (Peng et al., 2025). Unlike prior methods, Clean Forcing directly learns the history-induced velocity gap while keeping the base frozen. With at most 340 clips and no real video, it matches or surpasses full retraining in drift reduction and adds no inference cost after merging.

3 Background

An autoregressive (AR) video model generates a video as KK latent chunks x=(x(1),…,x(K))x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(K)}), each containing ff frames, conditioned on a text prompt cc:

pθ​(x∣c)=∏k=1Kpθ​(x(k)∣h(k),c),h(k)=x(<k),p_{\theta}(x\mid c)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{\theta}\!\left(x^{(k)}\mid h^{(k)},c\right),\qquad h^{(k)}=x^{(<k)}, (1)

where θ\theta denotes the pretrained model parameters and h(k)h^{(k)} is the history of committed chunks. Block-causal attention restricts each chunk to itself and its history, whose representations are stored in a KV cache. Each conditional is modeled by flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023). Given a clean latent chunk x0x_{0}, Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and noise level σt∈[0,1]\sigma_{t}\in[0,1] at solver step tt, the noisy state is zt=(1−σt)​x0+σt​ϵz_{t}=(1-\sigma_{t})x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon. The network vθ​(zt,h,t)v_{\theta}(z_{t},h,t) predicts the path velocity and is trained with ℒFM=𝔼x0,ϵ,t​‖vθ​(zt,h,t)−(ϵ−x0)‖22\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\epsilon,t}\|v_{\theta}(z_{t},h,t)-(\epsilon-x_{0})\|_{2}^{2}. At inference, each chunk is initialized from noise and denoised by integrating d​zd​σ=vθ\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}\sigma}=v_{\theta} from σ=1\sigma=1 to 00 over TT solver steps, then committed to the history.

Exposure bias. The model is trained on clean histories but conditioned on its own imperfect outputs at inference, leading to different conditional distributions under the model’s generated rollout history hgenh_{\mathrm{gen}} and the reference history hcleanh_{\mathrm{clean}}: pθ​(x(k)∣hgen,c)≠pθ​(x(k)∣hclean,c)p_{\theta}(x^{(k)}\mid h_{\mathrm{gen}},c)\neq p_{\theta}(x^{(k)}\mid h_{\mathrm{clean}},c) (Ranzato et al., 2016; Schmidt, 2019; Ning et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2025). Because each generated chunk becomes part of the history, errors compound across KK chunks into O⁡(K2​ε)O(K^{2}\varepsilon) cumulative error, manifesting as progressive quality drift over longer rollouts (Ross et al., 2011). Our goal is to align these conditional distributions during inference, such that pθ​(x(k)∣hgen,c)≈pθ​(x(k)∣hclean,c)p_{\theta}(x^{(k)}\mid h_{\mathrm{gen}},c)\approx p_{\theta}(x^{(k)}\mid h_{\mathrm{clean}},c).

4 Clean Forcing

Clean Forcing converts our measurement into a learned corrector in three steps (Fig. 2). First, we show that the velocity error induced by a drifted history is largely systematic across noise seeds and can therefore be corrected by a deterministic function (§4.1; panel 1). Second, we train a lightweight LoRA on the frozen base to map the drifted-history velocity to the model’s counterfactual clean-history prediction at the same noisy state (§4.2; panel 2). Third, we close the train–inference gap through DAgger-style data aggregation and a drift-contraction objective (§4.3; panel 3). Finally, we show that clean references need not come from real videos because the same checkpoint can generate its own drift-free supervision in bidirectional mode (§4.4).

At inference, the corrected velocity is

vrect=vθ+α⁡(vθ+LoRA−vθ),v_{\mathrm{rect}}=v_{\theta}+\alpha\left(v_{\theta+\mathrm{LoRA}}-v_{\theta}\right), (2)

where α\alpha controls the correction strength. Setting α=1\alpha=1 recovers the LoRA-merged forward pass and therefore adds no inference overhead. The measured systematic fraction α∗​(t)\alpha^{*}(t) provides a principled correction strength at each solver step. It remains nearly constant at ≈0.95\approx 0.95 on our base model, so we use the full merged correction without a time-dependent gating schedule.

4.1 Drift Is a Systematic Velocity Error

For each state ztz_{t} reached by a drifted rollout, we evaluate the frozen model twice while changing only the history: Δ⁡(zt,t)=vθ​(zt,hclean,t)−vθ​(zt,hgen,t)\Delta(z_{t},t)=v_{\theta}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{clean}},t)-v_{\theta}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{gen}},t). Because both predictions use the same state, Δ\Delta isolates the counterfactual effect of history corruption. We measure the fraction of this velocity gap that is reproducible across noise seeds as

α∗​(t)=‖𝔼s​[Δs]‖22‖𝔼s​[Δs]‖22+Vars⁡(Δs),\alpha^{*}(t)=\frac{\|\mathbb{E}_{s}[\Delta_{s}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\mathbb{E}_{s}[\Delta_{s}]\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Var}_{s}(\Delta_{s})}, (3)

where ss indexes noise seeds and Vars⁡(Δs)=𝔼s​[‖Δs−𝔼s​[Δs]‖22]\operatorname{Var}_{s}(\Delta_{s})=\mathbb{E}_{s}[\|\Delta_{s}-\mathbb{E}_{s}[\Delta_{s}]\|_{2}^{2}]. Across all noise levels, the measured systematic fraction α∗​(t)∈[0.89,0.99]\alpha^{*}(t)\in[0.89,0.99] on three base models (Fig. 7). Thus, approximately 95%95\% of the history-induced velocity error is systematic, indicating that a deterministic function can learn to correct it. Because α∗​(t)\alpha^{*}(t) remains close to 11 throughout denoising, we apply the full correction at every step without a gating schedule, as validated in §5. The same checkpoint produces clean clips in bidirectional single-shot mode, which serve as our clean histories (§4.4), indicating that drift arises from autoregressive rollout rather than limited model capacity.

4.2 One-Step Counterfactual-Teacher Correction (rϕr_{\phi})

We train the corrector to match the frozen model’s clean-history prediction at the same noisy state:

ℒCF=𝔼k,t,ϵ​[‖vθ+LoRA​(zt,hgen,t)−vθ​(zt,hclean,t)‖22‖vθ​(zt,hclean,t)−vθ​(zt,hgen,t)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CF}}=\mathbb{E}_{k,t,\epsilon}\left[\frac{\left\|v_{\theta+\mathrm{LoRA}}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{gen}},t)-v_{\theta}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{clean}},t)\right\|_{2}^{2}}{\left\|v_{\theta}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{clean}},t)-v_{\theta}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{gen}},t)\right\|_{2}^{2}}\right]. (4)

Each training example selects a chunk x0x_{0} from a cached drifted rollout and re-noises it as zt=(1−σt)​x0+σt​ϵz_{t}=(1-\sigma_{t})x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon. The student evaluates ztz_{t} under hgenh_{\mathrm{gen}} with the corrector active, while the frozen teacher evaluates the same state under hcleanh_{\mathrm{clean}}. The denominator normalizes each example by the magnitude of its original drift gap. We report R2=1−ℒCFR^{2}=1-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CF}}, the average fraction of each example’s drift gap that the corrector closes. The corrector rϕr_{\phi} consists of rank-16 LoRA adapters on the self-attention projections, totaling 5.95.9M parameters (0.4%0.4\% of the base). We initialize each LoRA output matrix BB to zero, so the corrected model initially matches the frozen base exactly.

Anchoring. Anchoring ztz_{t} to a ground-truth trajectory instead can pair the generated history with a state from a different scene, producing a mismatched correction that increases drift in our experiments (§5). Under flow matching, the gap between the predicted clean latents scales linearly with the noise level, ‖Δ​x^0‖=σt​‖Δ​v‖\|\Delta\hat{x}_{0}\|=\sigma_{t}\|\Delta v\| (Fig. 2, panel 1).

4.3 Closed-Loop Training: DAgger and Drift Contraction

The one-step objective is trained on states visited by the uncorrected model but deployed on states visited by the corrected model, creating the covariate shift addressed by DAgger (Ross et al., 2011). To close this gap, we augment one-step training with DAgger aggregation and drift contraction.

DAgger aggregation. We regenerate paired training data with the current corrector active and add it to the existing dataset. Training then samples from this aggregated pool, exposing the corrector to states encountered during its own rollouts.

Drift contraction. From the corrected velocity, we estimate the clean latent as

x^0=zt−σt​vθ+LoRA​(zt,hgen,t).\hat{x}_{0}=z_{t}-\sigma_{t}v_{\theta+\mathrm{LoRA}}(z_{t},h_{\mathrm{gen}},t). (5)

We append x^0\hat{x}_{0} to the student history while retaining its gradient, then evaluate the normalized velocity gap on the re-noised next chunk x0+x_{0}^{+}:

ℒcon=ℒCF​(x0+,hgen⊕x^0,hclean⊕x¯0).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CF}}\bigl(x_{0}^{+};\,h_{\mathrm{gen}}\oplus\hat{x}_{0},\,h_{\mathrm{clean}}\oplus\bar{x}_{0}\bigr).

Here ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation, and x¯0\bar{x}_{0} is the clean reference chunk corresponding to x^0\hat{x}_{0}. Backpropagating through x^0\hat{x}_{0} trains the corrector to reduce the drift its committed prediction causes in the next chunk. The total closed-loop training loss is

ℒCL=ℒCF+λcon​ℒcon,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CL}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CF}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{con}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}, (6)

where ℒcon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} denotes the drift-contraction loss and λcon=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{con}}=0.5. Ablations in §5 show that both DAgger aggregation and drift contraction contribute to reducing long-horizon drift.

4.4 Clean-History Sources

The teacher requires clean histories, but these need not come from real videos. We evaluate three settings: (a) real clips, for which 40 clips suffice; (b) prompts only, where the checkpoint generates single-shot 5 s clips in bidirectional mode, which avoids autoregressive drift and provides clean self-supervision; and (c) no clean reference, where reference-free distribution matching fails to reduce drift (§5). Because a bidirectional checkpoint can extend an existing clip but cannot reliably generate from a prompt alone, we causally adapt it using the same synthetic clips and merge the adapter into the base (Appendix A), after which Clean Forcing corrects the remaining drift, with the two providing complementary improvements (§5).

5 Experiments

Implementation details. Our main base is Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (Wan Team, 2025), configured with block-causal attention over 3-latent chunks, a rolling 21-latent KV cache, and a 20-step solver at 832×480832{\times}480, 16 fps, CFG 66, and shift 88. The adapted base has the rank-64 causal adapter from §4.4 merged into its weights. We also evaluate Wan2.1-T2V-14B, which is 10×10\times larger (Appendix G.1), and an independently trained Causal Forcing checkpoint (Zhu et al., 2026) (Appendix G.2). The corrector places rank-16 LoRA adapters on the qq, kk, vv, and oo self-attention projections in all 30 DiT blocks, yielding 5.95.9M trainable parameters (0.4%0.4\% of the base). We initialize the LoRA output matrices to zero, use unit scaling, and train with AdamW at learning rates of 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4} for one-step correction and 2×10−42{\times}10^{-4} for closed-loop training. The causal adapter uses the same projections and a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}. Training uses at most 340 clips (40 real and 300 synthetic); the zero-real-video variant uses only the 300 synthetic clips, versus the 5555K source clips and 8181K generated trajectories of Po et al. (2025). The full pipeline, including generation of teacher clips, takes approximately one day on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU in bf16 and requires at least 48 GB of GPU memory (Appendix A).

Baselines. We compare three groups. (A) Methods implemented on our base: context noising with σ=0.2\sigma=0.2 (Chen et al., 2024; Skywork AI, 2025), history guidance with w=1.2w=1.2 (Song et al., 2025), and pathwise test-time correction under both published schedules (Xiang et al., 2026). We run these methods on the adapted base using their published hyperparameters. Table 4 documents the implementations and three in-domain controls evaluated on the unadapted base: DMD supervision without clean references (Yu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2024), naive fine-tuning, and architecture variants. We also evaluate the independently adapted Causal Forcing checkpoint (Zhu et al., 2026) with and without our correction under the same protocol, since its release does not specify an inference configuration (Table 8). (B) Released checkpoints: Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025) and SkyReels-V2 (Skywork AI, 2025) are evaluated on the same 128 prompts. (C) Published results: BAgger (Po et al., 2025) is reported on the same calibrated scale but using a different base and prompt set, making direct comparison indicative. All groups use the Wan2.1-1.3B architecture (Appendix B).

Evaluation metrics. Our main evaluation uses 50 s generations from 128 LLM-refined MovieGenVideoBench prompts (Polyak et al., 2024) held out from training. All methods use identical prompt and seed pairs (Table 1). We report official VBench scores (Huang et al., 2024) and Δ\Delta-drift, defined as the MUSIQ score (Ke et al., 2021) of the first 20% of frames minus that of the full video (Zhang et al., 2025; Po et al., 2025). To check for metric-specific gains, we also report Δ\DeltaQualityDrift (Meng et al., 2026), quality over time (Yin et al., 2025), color shift, anchored survival (Xiang et al., 2026), and temporal LPIPS (Table 11; Appendix C). We compare dynamic degree and flicker against ground-truth clips. Error bars show the SEM across prompts. Scoring every frame changes MUSIQ by at most 1.81.8 and Δ\Delta-drift by at most 0.260.26, without changing the Δ\Delta-drift ranking. Appendix I additionally evaluates in-domain extension using 5 held-out clips extended by 48 latent frames with 3 paired seeds (Table 10), and short-horizon quality using 200 VBench prompts at 5 s (Table 12).

5.1 Results

Quantitative results. Table 1 validates our claim that a frozen base can match the drift reduction of models fully retrained at cluster scale. On the shared base, Clean Forcing reduces Δ\Delta-drift from +11.27+11.27 to +1.65+1.65 without real video and to −0.16\mathbf{-0.16} with only 40 real clips, indicating no measurable quality decay over 50 s. Against released, retrained models evaluated on identical prompts, the ++real variant is lower by more than 3 SEM, while the zero-real variant ties them using over 150×150\times less data. Even the zero-real variant outperforms the best published corrective fine-tuning result on the calibrated scale, with +1.65+1.65 versus +3.57+3.57 for R3†.

Drift reduction does not trade off overall quality. Every VBench dimension improves except motion smoothness, which decreases by 2.02.0 points as dynamic degree rises from 29.729.7 to 49.249.2: frame-difference metrics reward stillness, so recovering motion costs smoothness (Appendix C). On our adapted base, Clean Forcing improves subject consistency and imaging quality by 15–16 points and raises prompt adherence from 58.858.8 to 70.370.3/69.969.9, comparable to the distilled model’s 70.170.1 (Table 13). Its aesthetic score reaches 61.461.4 on this base and a table-leading 62.962.9 on the Causal-Forcing base. Quality also remains stable when the same videos are evaluated at 10, 30, and 50 s (Table 14). SkyReels remains strongest in consistency and smoothness, two dimensions that benefit from large-scale base training.

All training-free interventions we evaluate increase drift relative to the base (+11.3+11.3): history guidance yields +20.6+20.6, the two pathwise TTC schedules yield +14.0+14.0 and +14.5+14.5, and context noising yields +12.1+12.1 (Appendix C). Among the methods in Table 1, only Clean Forcing achieves Δ\Delta-drift below +2+2 without retraining the base at cluster scale (Huang et al., 2025; Skywork AI, 2025).

Clean Forcing recipe transfers without model-specific changes or hyperparameter search. On the independently adapted Causal-Forcing base, it reduces drift by 77%77\%, from +11.99+11.99 to +2.80+2.80, recovers all consistency and aesthetic dimensions to the level of our adapted base, achieves the highest dynamic degree in the table at 70.370.3, and restores prompt adherence to 71.071.0 (Appendix G.2). At 10×10\times scale, it removes 94%94\% of drift on Wan2.1-14B without changing dynamic degree (Appendix G.1). With a lower correction strength, it also reduces drift in two additional autoregressive world models: HY-WorldPlay (Sun et al., 2025) and the OmniDreams driving model (Basant et al., 2026) (Appendix G.3).

Qualitative results. Figure 3 shows when drift emerges: the base and all training-free heuristics degrade within 15 s, while both Clean Forcing variants remain stable through 50 s. Figure 4 shows the corresponding frames, in which the base exhibits saturation burnout, the heuristics cause fragmentation or freezing, and Self Forcing develops a late color shift. Appendix K presents six additional prompts, Figures 8 and 10 show the same comparison at 14B and on the Causal-Forcing base, and videos for all figure prompts are linked from the project page. Compared with models retrained at cluster scale on the same prompts, Clean Forcing achieves the lowest drift and highest aesthetic score and ranks second in subject and background consistency, imaging quality, and MUSIQ.

Efficiency analysis. At full correction strength, the corrected velocity is exactly the LoRA-merged forward pass, so rϕr_{\phi} folds into the base weights (Hu et al., 2022) without changing computation, parameter count, peak memory, or NFE (Δ​NFE=0\Delta\mathrm{NFE}=0). Wall-clock latency is statistically indistinguishable from the base (Table 5 in Appendix E), with a 3.5%3.5\% increase and Welch p=0.40p=0.40. Merging with a nonconstant schedule α∗​(t)\alpha^{*}(t) is discussed in Appendix E. An unfused corrector adds 35%35\% latency, while history guidance doubles NFE and pathwise TTC requires additional denoising passes. Thus, only retraining and Clean Forcing add no inference overhead, and only Clean Forcing is also cheap to train.

User study. Following Yin et al. (2025), 33 raters (29 from Prolific and 4 directly invited) each evaluated 15 randomized pairs of 10 s late-window excerpts (t=40t=40–5050 s), with attention checks and at least 5 ratings per pair, yielding 858 judgments. The ++real variant of Clean Forcing is preferred over the base in 93.0%\mathbf{93.0\%} of judgments and over Self Forcing in 83.9%\mathbf{83.9\%}, both at p<10−16p<10^{-16}. Its comparison with SkyReels-V2 is not significantly different from an even split (42.7%42.7\%, p=0.09p=0.09), although SkyReels-V2 is preferred for stability and outputs at 24 fps versus 16 fps for all other methods. Table 16 reports per-question results, and Appendix J details the protocol and catch-trial analysis.
